query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 0.7 mol of aluminum into a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will improve its mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance by triggering an FCC-to-BCC phase transformation and promoting the formation of protective Al-oxide layers.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a predominantly FCC structure and no significant protective oxide layer formation.
generation.intervention: Alloy composition modification via the addition of ~0.7 mol Al into the CoCrFeNi matrix.
generation.conditions: Tested at room temperature under conditions typical for aerospace fastener applications, including exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., saline solutions) and mechanical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The induced phase transformation from FCC to BCC along with the development of stable, passivating aluminum oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: The moderate Al addition causes lattice distortions that favor the formation of a BCC phase, which is inherently more resistant to dislocation creep, while also creating a thin, protective Al-oxide layer on the surface that enhances corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi alloy, the Al-modified alloy will exhibit reduced room-temperature creep rates and improved corrosion resistance, thereby increasing overall mechanical durability.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi alloy without Al addition that retains a primarily FCC structure and exhibits lower creep resistance and weaker passivation against corrosion.
generation.boundary: The improvements should manifest under room-temperature and aerospace fastener service conditions, though the quantitative gains may depend on processing history and environmental specifics. Significant deviation from these conditions may limit the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitudes of the improvements in creep resistance and corrosion resistance are not precisely defined and may vary with slight changes in processing parameters and testing methods.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of aerospace fasteners: one set made from the base CoCrFeNi alloy and one set with the addition of ~0.7 mol Al. Subject both sets to room-temperature nanoindentation creep tests and corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution). Ensure that the mechanical processing history (e.g., casting, heat treatment) is identical for both sets.
measurements: Measure creep rates (displacement vs. time under fixed load) via nanoindentation to assess room-temperature creep resistance.
Obtain potentiodynamic polarization curves to determine corrosion current density (Icorr) and corrosion potential (Ecorr).
Perform microstructural analyses (e.g., XRD or TEM) to confirm the FCC-to-BCC phase transformation and the presence of Al-oxide layers.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in room-temperature creep rates and/or improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., lower Icorr and more noble Ecorr) compared to the untreated alloy, or if no clear FCC-to-BCC transformation and passivating oxide formation can be observed, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a new class of alloys that consist of more than four alloying elements in close to equiatomic concentrations (). The diverse compositional possibilities of HEAs, combined with appropriate heat treatment conditions, offer the potential to develop new alloys with a combination of remarkable properties such as outstanding mechanical properties, high-hydrogen absorption capacity, and robust resistance to corrosion and radiation (). The refractory HEAs (RHEAs) based on refractory elements were proposed by Senkov et al. () as a new class of high-temperature structural alloys that might surpass the capabilities of nickel-based superalloys. RHEAs are emerging as prominent contenders in diverse industries, notably in the nuclear and aerospace sectors (, ).

With the rapid development of high-temperature sectors such as the aerospace and power generation industries, the demand for metallic materials that maintain exceptional mechanical properties under high-temperature conditions has significantly increased. Recent studies have revealed that refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements such as tungsten (W), molybdenum (Mo), niobium (Nb), and tantalum (Ta) exhibit superior high-temperature strength and good fatigue resistance, surpassing the currently used nickel-based superalloys [,]. However, RHEAs, such as the MoNbTaVW alloy [], typically have high densities and exhibit brittleness at room temperature, which limits their application scope. The addition of aluminum (Al), with its low density and large atomic radius, induces lattice distortions when forming solid solutions with refractory metals, reducing the system’s free energy, thereby enhancing solution strengthening effects. Therefore, Al is often added to RHEAs to reduce alloy density and improve specific strength. Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.

reading.lever: Introduce an optimized, moderate Al addition (≈0.7 mol) into a CoCrFeNi-based HEA to trigger FCC-to-BCC transformation and form protective passivating oxides.
reading.why: This intervention builds on evidence that Al addition enhances creep resistance and corrosion protection in related HEA systems, directly addressing fastener performance gaps.
